objective.statement: Name an interval by counting letter names.
successCriteria: I know an interval is the distance between two notes.
I count both notes when I name an interval by number.
I can name an interval from a 2nd to an octave above a note.

explanation.text: An interval is the distance between two notes. At Grade 1 we name it by a number only. To find the number, count the letter names from the lower note to the upper note, counting both of them.

music.textAlternative: Two notes in the treble clef, C and E, with the letters in between: C D E.

explanation.caption: C up to E: C, D, E. That counts three letter names, so it is a 3rd.

music.textAlternative: Two notes in the treble clef, C and G: C D E F G.

explanation.caption: C up to G: C, D, E, F, G. Five letter names, so it is a 5th.

explanation.text: The same note twice is a unison (1st). Counting up to the next note with the same letter name is an octave, the 8th.
Always count the lower note as 1. That is the most common slip: counting from the next note instead.

music.textAlternative: A row of eight notes from C to C, so each can be heard as an interval above the first C.

steps: Tap the first C, then the second note, D: that is a 2nd (C D).
Tap C then E: a 3rd (C D E). C then G: a 5th.
Tap C then the top C: an octave (8th), the same note name an octave higher.
demonstration.textAlternative: A C major scale in the treble clef, used to hear intervals above the first note C.

guided.prompt: Give the number of this interval (for example, 3rd). The lower note is the tonic of D major.

music.textAlternative: Two semibreves in the treble clef: D4, then C♯5 above it.

hints: Count both notes.
Use the notes of the scale.
Count every letter name from the bottom note to the top note, including both.

mistakes.counted-one-end-only: Count both notes: the bottom note is 1, then every letter name up to and including the top note.
mistakes.quality-from-wrong-key: Judge the quality by imagining the major scale on the lower note. Is the top note in it?
mistakes.compound-arithmetic: An octave plus a 5th is a 12th, not a 13th: the shared note is counted only once.
mistakes.enharmonic-spelling: That sounds right, but intervals depend on letter names. Check how many letter names the interval spans.
mistakes.augmented-diminished-swap: Is the interval a semitone bigger or smaller than the major/perfect version? Bigger means augmented; smaller means diminished (or minor).

feedback.fallback: Not quite. Count the letter names first, then compare with the major scale on the lower note.

guided.prompt: In F major, which note is a 6th above the tonic?

C.reason: C is a 5th above the tonic. Count the tonic itself as 1 when you count up.

E.reason: E is a 7th above the tonic. Count the tonic itself as 1 when you count up.

hints: Count the tonic as 1.
Count the tonic as 1 and go up the scale one letter at a time until you reach the number.

recap: An interval is the distance between two notes.
Count the letter names, including the lower and the upper note.
At Grade 1 only the number is named, not the quality.

mastery.completion: The lesson is complete when every step has been answered correctly (retries allowed). Only first-attempt, hint-free independent answers count as mastery evidence; guided steps never do.
